The self-attention mechanism has become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing, with its performance heavily influenced by the network's dimensional parameters. This study investigates how the dimensions of query, key, and value vectors—specifically depth and width—affect the model's ability to capture representations. We demonstrate that the key and value dimensions dictate the maximum representational capacity of self-attention, whereas the query dimension determines the specific nature of that representation. We further show that query width constrains the model's capacity to distinguish between different representations, findings which are supported both theoretically and empirically.

This study details the synthesis of BiFeO$_3$ nanoparticles using a sol-gel method at reduced temperatures, followed by calcination at 600°C. The resulting nanoparticles exhibit a cubic perovskite structure with a rhombohedral distortion, a particle size of approximately 10 nm, and a narrow size distribution. The material demonstrates a room-temperature magnetization of 1.0 emu/g, which is notably higher than that of bulk BiFeO$_3$ and comparable to values observed in larger nanoparticle sizes. Furthermore, the sample shows strong photocatalytic activity in hydrogen production and the degradation of methylene blue dye under visible light irradiation. The nanoparticle's superior performance is attributed to its small size, high surface-to-volume ratio, and the absence of secondary phases. These findings indicate that the synthesized BiFeO$_3$ nanoparticles are promising candidates for applications in spintronics, photocatalysis, and energy storage.

We examine a toy ${\rm SU}(6)$ model featuring a single scalar doublet and a single right-handed neutrino per generation, where Yukawa couplings are organized into ${\rm SU}(3)_{\rm f}$ representations. This framework successfully reproduces the observed hierarchical patterns of fermion masses and mixing angles. By analyzing the mass spectrum of the resulting ${\rm SU}(6)$ representations, we derive predictions for the masses of the down quarks, up quarks, and right-handed neutrinos, as well as the mixing angles among these particles. Specifically, we determine the bottom quark mass and the right-handed neutrino mass spectrum, which in turn allows us to calculate the mass of the tau neutrino. Utilizing the experimentally measured tau neutrino mass, we extract a prediction for the tau lepton mass. The resulting theoretical value aligns closely with the experimentally determined tau particle mass.

We introduce a new approach to the 3D reconstruction of generic objects held in hands, a task that is difficult due to the wide variety of object shapes and the complex, occluding interactions between the object and the hand. Our method utilizes a 3D convolutional neural network to simultaneously reconstruct both the object and the hand from a single RGB image. The system jointly learns to predict 3D point clouds for both objects and hands, explicitly modeling the physical contact and occlusion between them. Our results demonstrate that this approach can reconstruct 3D generic items from manual poses with high accuracy.

The Ca-K index, a standard metric for quantifying chromospheric activity, is traditionally calculated by normalizing the continuum flux at 393.37 nm against the continuum flux at 396.85 nm. This study introduces a revised index, defined as the ratio of continuum flux at 393.37 nm to the continuum flux at 396.85 nm. We utilized a dataset spanning 1910 to 2010 obtained from the Kodaikanal Observatory, which was originally captured with uniform contrast. This contrast was converted into a linear scale using a newly developed algorithm. This approach allowed us to track variations in the Ca-K index over the last century, revealing a significant decline in Ca-K values during the 1950s and 2010s. This reduction aligns with a corresponding decrease in sunspot numbers, indicating a long-term trend of declining solar activity. Furthermore, we observed a correlation between the Ca-K index and the 10.7 cm radio flux, noting that this relationship strengthens during periods of high solar activity.

The study of the rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ represents a significant opportunity to investigate the $\Sigma^+$ hyperon's internal structure and to probe for new physics beyond the Standard Model. This analysis utilizes a Monte Carlo simulation to evaluate the feasibility of detecting this decay at the LHCb experiment. The study examines the decay's kinematics, establishes its branching ratio, and determines the expected number of decay events given a specific integrated luminosity. The results indicate that observing this decay is feasible at LHCb, provided an integrated luminosity of 1 fb$^{-1}$ is accumulated.

Test complexity serves as a fundamental metric for evaluating the quality of test suites. While existing methods for calculating this measure often depend on program execution, they are unsuitable for large-scale distributed environments. This paper introduces a novel distributed algorithm designed to compute test complexity by leveraging the notion of "test depth." A test is defined as "test depth" zero if it executes a single method; otherwise, its depth corresponds to the maximum depth of any method it calls plus one. This definition enables a segmented approach to calculating test complexity, where each node in a distributed cluster computes the sum of complexities for a specific subset of tests. This strategy significantly enhances scalability, allowing the system to process massive test collections. We have implemented this algorithm in a Java-based framework and validated its effectiveness through experiments using extensive test suites from the TeraSort project.

We investigate the dynamics of the magnetization vector within an embedded magnetic nanoparticle, focusing specifically on the phenomenon known as "rejuvenation." This study reveals that when the nanoparticle's magnetization vector is organized into clusters, the range of external field histories exhibiting rejuvenation expands significantly. Furthermore, we demonstrate that within such a clustered configuration, the system's energy landscape consists of numerous metastable states, each characterized by distinct cluster arrangements.

Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising approach for distributed machine learning, enabling the aggregation of client models to train a global model without exposing raw data. While recent research has explored federated social networks by leveraging the inherent trust relationships between clients to enhance FL efficiency, current methods typically depend on a central hub. This reliance creates a single point of failure and raises privacy concerns regarding data sent to the central server. This paper introduces a new framework for FL over social networks that eliminates the central hub, relying solely on mutual trust among clients. We propose a novel algorithm that uses a weighted aggregation strategy, where trust scores between clients determine the contribution of each model to the global model. Additionally, we develop a distributed algorithm to compute these trust scores using only local model updates, ensuring that no single client can manipulate the results. Experimental evaluations on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable FL performance to existing hub-based methods while eliminating the need for a central server.

This study presents a sequential categorization model designed for short texts, employing recurrent and convolutional neural networks to analyze text instances step-by-word. The model integrates a recurrent neural network (RNN) with convolutional layers, which are optimized for short-text classification, to process input sequentially at the word level. We evaluate the model's performance on the short-text categorization task using the AG News dataset. The results indicate that our approach achieves a higher accuracy of 89.0% compared to the standard 84.0% accuracy of traditional bag-of-words methods.

This paper presents a theoretical framework for analyzing telecentric Fabry-P\'erot resonators, where the parallel plates are substituted with optical systems composed of collimating lenses. The study derives the effective cavity length and the corresponding round-trip phase shift, accounting for the refractive index of the medium situated between the lenses. Furthermore, the analysis examines the influence of the lens focal length on the system's effective length and the angular divergence of the output beam. The proposed analytical expressions are benchmarked against numerical simulations, demonstrating excellent agreement. The derived formulas are subsequently applied to evaluate the performance of two specific resonator configurations: a resonant lens system and a resonant etalon equipped with a telescope.

This study investigates pairings of binary sequences of length $n$ that yield an even number of even positions. We introduce the pairing counts for sequences containing exactly $k$ ones, demonstrating a connection between these counts and the Apéry numbers. Furthermore, we establish a bijal between such pairings and a specific configuration of lattice paths.

The Codelet Framework is a lightweight, object-oriented, and distributed parallel programming model that offers a simple and efficient way to create distributed applications. It is designed to be hardware-agnostic, abstracting away hardware details, yet it provides enough flexibility to express hardware-specific requirements. This paper details the implementation of a runtime system that maps Codelet framework applications onto commercial chiplet-based accelerators. We describe a methodology for translating a codelet framework application into a set of chiplet programs, each tailored for execution on the processor or specific accelerator. We also outline the design of a runtime system that facilitates this chiplet-specific programming and discuss the key architectural features of the runtime.

Mixture cure models are frequently employed to analyze survival data within populations containing a non-treated (cured) fraction. A prevalent issue with this approach is the instability of standard kernel-based estimators for the cumulative distribution function of the latent distribution, stemming from the non-smooth nature of the standard kernel estimator. To address this, we introduce a semiparametric framework that incorporates a presmoothing technique to mitigate these estimator instabilities. Through theoretical analysis, we derive the asymptotic normality of the proposed method and demonstrate, via simulations, that it achieves enhanced performance in terms of bias and variance. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical application of the method using data from a clinical trial.

This study examines the nonlocal distance dimension, originally defined by G. Exoo in 1982, by extending the concept to include non-diagonal terms. We demonstrate that for any graph $G$, the nonlocal dimension is bounded above by $|V(G)| - 1 + \delta$, where $\delta$ represents the maximum degree of $G$. Furthermore, we establish that for any tree $T$, the nonlocal dimension equals $|V(T)| - 1$. We also derive an upper bound for the nonlocal dimension of weighted graphs and investigate how this dimension relates to the Lovász $\theta$ function.

The rise of in-memory computing (IMC) has introduced a novel class of side-channel attacks that target memory architectures directly. This study introduces a new side-channel methodology designed to breach IMC frameworks by exploiting the unique characteristics of their processing mechanisms. The attacks leverage the inherent unpredictability of memory access patterns, which are dictated by the execution flow of the input code, to probe the system's processing capabilities. This approach is validated on two prominent frameworks: the Intel-based framework and the one developed by the University of Notre Dame. The proposed attack demonstrates a significant performance advantage over existing methods, achieving up to 100 times greater accuracy.

We introduce a framework designed to reduce the polarization kernels associated with the scattering of two photons against each other. This method leverages partial-wave expansion combined with rotational invariance, along with the specific polarizations of the incoming photons, to perform these reductions. This technique proves especially valuable for calculating kernels relevant to the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and the Large-Scale Structure (LSS). We demonstrate this approach by applying it to the production of polarized photons during the scattering of a photon pair against the Primordial Black Hole (PBH) field.

Seismic data are frequently corrupted by self-similar, blind-spot, and transient noise, which hampers the accuracy of subsequent geological interpretations. While blind-spot noise is a prevalent issue, it remains difficult to mitigate because it is not explicitly recorded in the dataset. This paper introduces a self-supervised transfer learning framework designed to reduce blind-spot noise in seismic data. The approach involves training a convolutional neural network (CNN) to identify and eliminate noise using self-supervised techniques on clean seismic data, followed by applying the same model to degraded data containing the target noise. The model's architecture is optimized to minimize the discrepancy between its output and the original clean data. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly reduces the power of the target noise in the processed seismic data.

This study examines the influence of charge asymmetry on the kinematics of $ep$ and $\bar ep$ scattering within the context of actual photon emission. The analysis focuses on the charge asymmetry observed in the rapidity distributions of emitted photons, specifically within the region of the transverse mass spectrum. The findings indicate that this asymmetry exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on transverse photon momentum, a feature that can be utilized to determine the momentum transfer in both $ep$ and $\bar ep$ scattering events.

The spin-orbit-coupling-driven Mott insulator Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ is a promising candidate for realizing the quantum spin Hall effect. This study employs scanning tunneling spectroscopy to investigate the electronic structure of Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ on a SrTiO$_3$ substrate. We observe a band gap of 0.4 eV and a low-energy satellite peak at 0.2 eV, which is attributed to spin-polaron formation. These findings are consistent with spin and charge density wave theories, which describe the Mott insulator spectrum as a combination of spin-polaron formation and band splitting. This theoretical alignment is further supported by the observation of a satellite peak in the STM data.

Causal mediation analysis seeks to quantify the extent to which a treatment influences an outcome through a specific intermediate variable. This study focuses on scenarios where both the treatment and the mediator are continuous, with the treatment affecting the outcome both directly and indirectly via the intermediate. We propose a straightforward estimator for the direct and indirect effects, grounded in the principle of stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA). This estimator is derived from the assumption that the treatment and mediator influence the outcome independently, given that the treatment and the mediator are known. This estimator is easy to calculate, requires no assumptions about the functional forms of the treatment and mediator, and is robust to unobserved confounders. Suicide stands as a critical global health challenge, with the majority of fatalities resulting from completed attempts. While significant progress has been made in developing tools to detect suicidal ideation through social media, existing resources are limited by a scarcity of annotated datasets, which hinders the development of effective detection systems. This paper introduces Robin, a new corpus comprising 1.2 million tweets labeled as suicidal or not, which is the most extensive English-language dataset of its kind. We detail the curation process, including the annotation protocol, and present initial findings from baseline experiments. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive analysis of the data's characteristics, addressing diversity and bias, and explore the dataset's potential applications in suicide prevention.

This study examines the difference equation $x_{n+1}=ax^\alpha_{n}+bx^\alpha_{n-1}$, where $a,b,\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, and specifically addresses the scenario where $0<\alpha \leq 2$. We establish sufficient conditions for solution boundedness and derive multiple sets of parameters that guarantee this behavior.

This study examines the Born-Infeld (BI) electrodynamics model, along with two additional variants derived from the BI framework, specifically within the context of general relativity. We investigate the physical viability of these theories by analyzing their charged black hole solutions, focusing on the existence of a cosmological horizon and an event horizon. Furthermore, we derive thermodynamic attributes for these solutions, such as entropy, temperature, and specific heat capacity, and analyze their behavior. Our findings indicate that the specific heat capacity serves as a key indicator for analyzing the stability of these black hole solutions.

This paper explores $k$-Sidon collections, defined as subsets $A$ within an additive group where all linear combinations $\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i x_i$ (with $x_i$ distinct from $A$) yield unique results for every integer $k \geq 2$ and coefficients $\lambda_i$. We establish that the maximal size of such a set in the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is bounded below by $\Omega(n^{1/k})$ and bounded above by $\Omega(n^{1/k}(\log n)^{k-1})$. Additionally, we derive a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/2k})$ for the cardinality of $k$-Sidon sets in non-abelian groups.

We examine the finite-temperature behavior of the magnetic susceptibility within the one-dimensional XY spin chain model, which is solved exactly via the transfer matrix method. By employing the exact solution, we demonstrate that the correlation length's spatial phase and spatial decay exponent exhibit universal scaling with temperature. Specifically, we derive the scaling exponents for these parameters as functions of the anisotropy parameter. Furthermore, we show that the magnetic susceptibility follows a scaling law with respect to temperature, wherein the scaling exponents for its amplitude and asymptotic value are determined by the exponents governing the spatial phase and decay of the correlation length.

The cooling-induced transition from a paramagnetic to a ferromagnetic state in Ising models is a critical area of research, particularly for spintronic applications. While numerous studies have examined this process, the influence of the starting temperature on simulation performance remains underexplored. This work analyzes how the initial temperature impacts simulation efficiency by comparing two established algorithms: Metropolis and Heat Bath. Simulations were conducted on square lattices with sizes ranging from 100×10 to 1000×100. The findings indicate that the Heat Bath algorithm generally outperforms the Metropolis method, with a key exception: when the lattice size is 100×100 and the starting temperature is 1.0, the Metropolis method yields faster outcomes.

We examine the Anderson localization of a one-dimensional quasicrystal system featuring power-order hopping, defined by the Hamiltonian $H = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \lambda |n|^{\alpha} c_n^\dagger c_{n+1} + \text{h.c.}$, where $\alpha > 0$ and the coupling constant $\lambda$ is quasi-periodic. Our analysis demonstrates that for any fixed $\alpha > 0$, there exist intervals of $\lambda$ values containing arbitrarily long sequences of consecutive eigenstates that are exponentially localized. Furthermore, we prove that the spectrum of $H$ is purely point-like, populated entirely by eigenstates, with an associated eigenvalue eigenfunctions exhibiting a singular continuous spectrum.

The majority of natural language processing (NLP) research centers on English, leaving a significant gap in resources for other languages. This paper introduces a comprehensive survey of NLP methodologies specifically designed for multilingual, task‑oriented conversational systems. We begin by examining current multilingual NLP strategies, covering approaches that handle multiple languages within single models as well as those employing separate models for each language. Next, we detail task‑focused dialog systems that address cross‑lingual challenges, including language‑independent representations, cross‑lingual transfer, and in‑domain adaptations. Finally, we identify key open‑ended research questions and suggest potential future directions for this field.

We introduce a probabilistic framework designed to identify splicing control mechanisms by analyzing differential splicing patterns. This approach leverages the fact that alternative splicing is regulated by the transcriptional machinery assembling at specific sites within introns and exons. By modeling the transcriptional machinery as a random walk, the framework incorporates the temporal dynamics of short-term regulation, allowing for the detection of multiple distinct control modes. Our analysis of the *Drosophila melanogaster* genome reveals that the majority of splicing events are governed by a single mechanism, whereas a minority exhibit concurrent regulation by two or more modes. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the underlying parameters of these control modes can be successfully inferred from the data.

However, the law does not define specific security protocols, leaving organizations to determine their own approaches. Consequently, numerous technical strategies have emerged to address data privacy requirements, yet it remains unclear which strategies are most effective for specific compliance tasks. This study aims to address this gap by investigating how practitioners select and execute these strategies. We conducted a qualitative study involving 12 data privacy engineers, utilizing a methodological framework that first identified 17 technical strategies through the analysis of 12 interviews and 12 workshops. We then used these strategies to analyze 12 additional interviews and 12 workshops to understand the factors influencing their selection and execution. We present a novel method for analyzing azimuthal correlations among multiple particles produced in high-energy $pA$ collisions. This approach utilizes a specific rank of azimuthal anisotropy, denoted as $v_{\lambda}$, to characterize the anisotropic flow of $n$-particle systems, where $\lambda$ represents the order of the correlation. The analysis demonstrates that $v_{\lambda}$ serves as a reliable metric for describing the azimuthal flow of $n$-particle systems in $pA$ interactions. Furthermore, we examine the behavior of these $n$-particle flow coefficients, $v_{\lambda}(n)$, as functions of collision centrality and multiplicity. Our findings indicate that the ratios $v_{\lambda}(n)/v_{\lambda}(n+1)$ for $pA$ collisions align well with predictions from the Color Glass Condensate model, which describes the small-x gluon distribution within a large-nucleus target.

The formation of light nuclei in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=3$ GeV is examined through a transport model that incorporates both coalescence and statistical hadronization mechanisms. The study investigates the impact of the initial nuclear density profile on particle yields, specifically comparing a uniform distribution to a distribution derived from a Woods-Saxon potential. The results indicate that light nuclei production arises from a combination of both mechanisms, with the initial nuclear density profile significantly influencing the coalescence process.

The study of exoplanetary environments is a rapidly expanding field that examines the interactions between planets and their surroundings. This research focuses on rocky exoplanets, which are categorized into three distinct groups: those with atmospheres, those without atmospheres, and those in the process of losing their atmospheres. The paper reviews the current observational data and theoretical models regarding the environmental conditions within these groups, with a specific focus on surface temperature, atmospheric composition, and surface characteristics.

This paper introduces a novel GPU-accelerated technique for rapidly computing inverse matrices, capable of handling both square and non-square matrices. The method builds upon the classical Givens rotation approach, extending it to arbitrary dimensions. The primary advantage of this technique is its ability to calculate inverse matrices significantly faster than traditional methods, particularly when the matrix to be inverted is iteratively updated.

We examine the impact of back reaction on the power spectrum of primordial curvature perturbations within the framework of ultra-slow-roll (USR) inflation. Our findings indicate that the amplitude of this spectrum is significantly enhanced due to back reaction effects, a conclusion that aligns with previous research. However, we demonstrate that the power spectrum's scale dependence is markedly altered by back reaction, a distinction from prior studies. Specifically, we find that the spectral tilt is suppressed by factors of 10 to 100 relative to standard predictions. Furthermore, we explore how back reaction affects the scale dependence of the bispectrum and observe that the spectral tilt of the bispectrum is substantially larger than that of the spectral tilt in the power spectrum.

This study addresses a variation of the linear assignment problem termed the Enhanced Selection Optimization Problem (ESOP). In this framework, a set of $n$ tasks must be completed by a workforce of $m$ workers, where the number of available agents exceeds the number of tasks ($m > n$). The objective is to identify a specific subset of exactly $n$ workers from this pool and assign them to all tasks such that the sum of their costs is minimized. Costs are defined by a matrix where the entry $c_{ij}$ represents the cost incurred when task $i$ is performed by worker $j$. The authors introduce a novel problem type and develop a polynomial-time algorithm capable of solving the ESOP optimally.

In survival analysis, the casebase framework serves as an alternative to the conventional cohort approach, offering a distinct perspective. While cohort studies focus on event frequencies relative to the population at risk, casebase studies analyze the probability of an event occurring within a specific timeframe. This framework is particularly advantageous for analyzing repeated events, as it circumvents the complexities associated with event dependency. The casebase framework offers two primary benefits: first, it simplifies the estimation of cumulative incidence functions, and second, it enables straightforward comparisons of event rates. Furthermore, the casebase methodology proves valuable in real-world scenarios, such as analyzing data from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute's ARIC study.

The recent surge in computing power has enabled the calculation of multi-loop Feynman integrals with varying order precisions, facilitating a deeper understanding of the accuracy physics inherent in these processes. This article examines the accuracy physics of multi-loop integrals, specifically focusing on two-point functions featuring a specific type of accuracy term. We also provide an overview of recent advancements in this field and discuss the corresponding theoretical and computational methodologies.

The increasing adoption of big data has driven a shift from traditional file systems to object storage, a method that enhances scalability and performance by decoupling the client from the file system namespace. This separation allows for the direct management of objects without file system overhead, enabling parallel access and improved efficiency. However, this approach introduces new challenges, notably the need to reconstruct a file from its constituent objects before it can be accessed. This research evaluates the performance of a distributed, Lustre-integrated object storage system against a native filesytem based on Lustre. The study analyzes various factors, including the number of constituent objects, file size, and the count of concurrent clients, to determine how these variables impact system performance.

The surge in electric vehicle (EV) usage has driven the creation of EV charging stations, yet the uneven distribution of these facilities and the scarcity of charging spots have created significant congestion. To address this, the proposed study introduces a digital reservation system designed to manage parking demand and optimize EV charging station utilization. The system operates on a first-come, first-served basis, allowing drivers to book parking spaces in advance. Furthermore, it incorporates a dynamic pricing model that adjusts rates according to real-time demand and occupancy levels. The study evaluates the system's effectiveness through a simulation of parking operations at the University of Texas at Austin, demonstrating that the online platform significantly enhances parking efficiency.

Linear complementary dual (LCD) codes represent a class of codes that are increasingly significant in the realm of cryptography. This study introduces a novel class of $q$-ary two-dimensional codes, termed generalized Tzvetkova-Malinovskaya (GTM) codes, which exhibit LCD properties. We demonstrate that every GTM code is an LCD code, establish the conditions under which GTM codes are self-orthogonal or self-dual, and outline methods for constructing GTM codes that are not isometric. Additionally, we examine the weight distributions of these codes and analyze how they evolve as they develop.

We demonstrate that the standard Einstein-Hilbert gravitational action can be derived from quantum loop corrections, utilizing a technique reminiscent of the Casimir effect. This approach involves quantizing a system of massless spin-1 fields, such as photons, within a curved spacetime. By analyzing the resulting corrections to the Maxwell action, we find that the leading term constitutes the standard Einstein-Hilbert action, thereby yielding classical general relativity.

Achieving a carbon-neutral future hinges on the large-scale adoption of renewable energy, yet this transition often incurs significant land-use costs. This study examines the trade-offs between electricity decarbonization and land consumption in the American West by evaluating the potential of concentrating solar power (CSP) and wind generation. We demonstrate that, despite the region's high potential for solar and wind deployment, meeting current electricity demand while eliminating fossil fuels would necessitate approximately 1.3 million hectares of new land. Although this area represents only about 10% of the total regional landmass, it is substantial enough to house roughly 1.5 million people. Our analysis reveals that relying exclusively on CSP would require five times more land than using only wind power. However, a hybrid mix of CSP and wind power offers a more balanced solution, reducing total land requirements by 20% to 40% compared to a wind-only strategy.

Cluster-randomized trials (CRTs) are frequently employed to evaluate vaccination efficacy. In these studies, entire clusters (such as schools or villages) receive either the vaccine or a control treatment, and individual participants within those clusters are assessed for outcomes. This design is utilized to examine both direct effects (protection of the vaccinated individual) and herd effects (protection of unvaccinated individuals within the treated group). This paper outlines the estimands for these two metrics, highlighting key challenges in their interpretation and suggesting that researchers should explicitly define the target population and time frame for these effects. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, direct and herd effects can be defined as average treatment effects on the treated (ATETs). Furthermore, we propose a strategy for combining data from both vaccinated and control clusters to estimate these effects, which proves particularly valuable in settings where randomization is imperfect.

The standardised Laplacian matrix, also known as the Laplacian with normalized rows, is a significant tool in spectral graph theory. This paper introduces the fractal standardised Laplacian matrix and examines its spectrum within specific fractal graph families. We determine the eigenvalues of the resulting spectrum by solving a fourth-order recurrence relation. Furthermore, we analyze applications of this new matrix, including its connection to the ordinary fractal Laplacian, as well as its role in defining both fractal and standard energy measures.

This study examines contextual linear gambits within a distributed framework, where multiple learners operate across varying contexts to collectively enhance their decision-making. Unlike the centralized paradigm, our distributed approach prevents context and action data from being shared among participants. We introduce a novel algorithm that enables learners to construct effective decision policies by exchanging only the upper quantile of their loss distributions. We demonstrate that this method achieves a regret bound of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$, where $K$ represents the number of learners and $T$ denotes the time horizon.

Digital Health Records (DHRs) serve as the primary repository for clinical data, yet their scarcity in machine learning applications stems from privacy concerns and the prohibitive costs of data acquisition. Consequently, synthetic DHRs are frequently employed to facilitate the development of predictive models. However, existing methods often fail to capture the full complexity of records, resulting in a loss of critical information. This study introduces a new approach to generating comprehensive synthetic DHRs by utilizing a multi-modal generative model. We applied this technique to create a dataset of Cystic Fibrosis patients, integrating diverse data types such as demographics, clinical observations, and laboratory results. The generated dataset was validated through statistical analysis and a patient selection task, both of which confirmed that the data retains its original complexity.

This study examines the decay $D^{0} \to K^{\mp} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{\mp}$ by analyzing the resonance structures within the $\bar{K}^{\mp} \pi^{\pm}$ and $\bar{K}^{\mp} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{\pm}$ subsystems. The analysis utilizes a data sample of $1.0 \times 10^{9}$ $B^{0} \to D^{0} K^{+} K^{-} \pi^{-}$ events collected by the BESIII detector at a center-of-mass energy of 3.773 GeV. The results indicate that the $D^{0} \to \bar{K}^{\mp} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{-}$ decay is dominated by the $K^{*}(892)^{-} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{-}$ mode, while the $D^{0} \to \bar{K}^{-} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{-}$ mode is dominated by the $K^{0}(890) \pi^{\pm} \pi^{-}$ mode.

Novelpy is an open-source Python package designed to evaluate the novelty of scientific publications and patent records within specific fields. The tool calculates an item's novelty by comparing it against a database of related documents, employing various metrics such as semantic similarity of titles and abstracts, keyword overlap, and patent claim similarity. Users can either integrate with the API of the European Patent Office's database or generate their own comparison dataset from sources including PubMed and Google Scholar. The package also provides a user-friendly interface for visualizing the results of these analyses.

We introduce a novel method for generating ultra-short laser pulses by employing cross-phase modulation (XPM) between a weak pulse and a strong one within a Kerr medium. This approach offers a viable alternative to conventional spectral broadening techniques that rely on intense self-phase modulation. We demonstrate that the resulting weak pulse exhibits a spectrum that is both spectrally broadened and temporally compressed, accompanied by a spatiotemporal evolution that can be precisely controlled by adjusting the relative delay and spatial overlap of the interacting pulses.

The primary challenge in cross-domain recommendation is to effectively transfer information from a source domain to a target domain, thereby enhancing recommendation performance. While existing methods often rely on adversarial learning to align feature spaces between domains, they typically demand extensive computational resources and time. To address this, we introduce Dual-Metric Learning (DML), a streamlined approach that employs two distinct metrics to capture the unique features of the source and target domains. By encouraging the preservation of domain-specific characteristics while simultaneously minimizing the distance between domain-invariant representations, DML achieves efficient cross-domain transfer. Empirical evaluations across three real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, delivering up to a 10.00% improvement in Hit Ratio and an 8.00% improvement in Mean Reciprocal Rank.

This study investigates the thermal transfer within two-dimensional, complex plasma bilayers using the two-dimensional Poisson-Boltzmann equation. The analysis focuses on the influence of the dielectric constant's anisotropy, specifically examining how variations in the ratio of perpendicular to parallel components affect the system. The findings indicate that increasing anisotropy leads to a reduction in the effective thermal conductivity coefficient.

This study addresses the identification of the components of the sum of two unordered data arrays. It demonstrates that the sum of two such arrays cannot be represented as the sum of any other pairs consisting of more than two components.

This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to enhance the quality of fluoroscopy images by utilizing a pair of adjacent frames. Leveraging the information from neighboring frames, the system reconstructs a high-quality image that exhibits reduced noise and improved spatial resolution. This enhanced output subsequently lowers the X-ray radiation exposure rate during the procedure. To achieve this, we developed a deep learning architecture comprising a denoising autoencoder, which is trained on a synthetic dataset to map noisy inputs to their clean counterparts. The autoencoder's encoder network functions as the generator within a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), while the decoder acts as the critic to evaluate and refine the generated results. The proposed method was validated on a 256x256 resolution synthetic dataset, and its efficacy was benchmarked against the DnCNN model.

We investigate the neutrino barrier phenomenon within leptophilic $U(1)$ frameworks, where the vacuum energy density for neutrinos is modified by the presence of background matter. This study examines the barrier's influence on the survival probability of electron neutrinos, specifically contrasting leptophilic $U(1)$ models with the standard $U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ framework. We find that the barrier is more pronounced in the $U(1)_{L_\mu-\chi_{L_\tau}}$ model, whereas it is significantly suppressed in the $U(1)_{L_e-L_\tau}$ model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the barrier's effect on electron neutrino survival probability is more pronounced in the $U(1)_{L_\mu-\chi_{L_\tau}}$ model, whereas it is significantly suppressed in the $U(1)_{L_e-\chi_{L_\tau}}$ model. This study examines the orbital dynamics of a planetary-mass companion orbiting a 100 solar mass star within the central parsec of the Milky Way. We model the system's evolution, accounting for gravitational influences from the central supermassive black hole and the surrounding stellar cluster. Our results indicate that the planetary body can undergo secular orbital decay, spiraling inward until tidal disruption occurs. The resulting debris is ejected at hypervelocity speeds, with the maximum velocity contingent upon the initial semi-major axis of the planetary orbit. We demonstrate that the hypervelocity stars generated by this mechanism possess a distinctively flat velocity distribution, with a median of approximately 100 km/s and a median eccentricity near 0.9. These characteristics align well with recent observations of high-velocity stars in the Milky Way.

We examine a class of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) featuring singular drift and diffusion coefficients that are subject to multiplicative noise. These equations are formulated as a "perturbed" variant of another SDE with a well-established well-posedness record. By applying a regularization technique, we demonstrate that the perturbed system retains weak uniqueness and possesses weak solutions. The approach relies on deriving uniform estimates for the densities of the diffusion components within the system.

We demonstrate that the definition of the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$ remains invariant under generic forcing extensions provided such extensions are defined by name forcing concepts. This result extends to a broader class of forcings that includes those used to add Cohen reals and random reals. Additionally, this method offers a streamlined demonstration of the preservation of Martin's axiom through name forcing.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have achieved significant success across numerous natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the substantial computational costs associated with fine-tuning these models for specific tasks often make it impractical to adapt them to new domains. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework called Adaptor, designed to efficiently transfer PLMs to new tasks and domains. Adaptor operates by maintaining a primary PLM for the host model while utilizing a set of lightweight, task-specific adapters to handle diverse applications. Central to the framework is a new objective function that dynamically adjusts PLM representations, thereby enhancing the model's adaptability to new tasks. Empirical evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that Adaptor outperforms existing adaptation methods, achieving gains of up to 2.5% in accuracy. Furthermore, the framework offers substantial efficiency improvements, reducing computational costs by as much as 90% compared to traditional fine-tuning approaches.

Traffic signs are essential for road safety, yet their recognition and categorization are critical for autonomous vehicles to navigate effectively. This paper introduces the Mapillary Traffic Sign Collection, a large-scale, global dataset comprising 100,000 annotated images of 800 traffic signs gathered from diverse environments. We provide an extensive analysis of the collection's composition and distribution across different regions. Additionally, we report the results of a baseline classification model trained on the data, achieving a top-1 accuracy of 90.1% and a top-5 accuracy of 95.4%.

Collaborative filtering (CF) is a well-established technique for recommender systems, yet it faces significant hurdles in real-world applications due to the difficulty of obtaining user-item interaction data. To address this, we introduce SelfCF, a self-supervised collaborative filtering framework capable of learning user and item representations without relying on explicit interactions. Our approach utilizes collaborative sorting to create a self-supervised task, where a user's preferences are modeled as a ranked list of items. Specifically, we propose a novel self-supervised sorting task that generates permutations of item lists to train a sorting model capable of reconstructing the original sequence. We further incorporate a self-distillation strategy to enhance the sorting model's performance. Comprehensive experiments on two collaborative filtering datasets demonstrate that SelfCF achieves state-of-the-art results in cold-start scenarios, even when trained on limited data.

Tevelev maps, which are particular kinds of branched covers of $\mathbb{P}^1$, are defined by their level—a measure of the number of times their image wraps around the target. This work investigates the possible values these numbers can take, termed "Tevelev levels." It demonstrates that for any given level $k$, there exists a broad class of such maps, and further, that the number of such maps is non-zero whenever $k$ is sufficiently large. These findings are established through a novel framework of "Tevelev arrangements," defined as the preimages of generic points under the respective maps.

This study examines a gapped Dirac semimetal characterized by dispersions that combine linear and parabolic behaviors. The model is derived from a general class of $C_4$-symmetric, two-dimensional, $d$-wave superconductors, which exhibit a $d$-wave superconducting phase within a specific region of the $d$-wave phase diagram. The resulting gapless Dirac dispersion is shaped by the interplay between the superconducting gap and the band curvature, which transitions from linear to parabolic as one moves from the center of the Brillouin zone toward its boundary. The authors analyze the effects of both a Zeeman field and an in-plane magnetic field on this system. The Zeeman field opens a gap in the Dirac dispersion, whereas an in-plane magnetic field induces a gapless Majorana mode at the sample edges.

Let $C$ represent a projective, smooth curve of genus $g \geq 2$ defined over an algebraically closed field $K$ with a characteristic not equal to 2. We consider $C$ as a semi-stable object within the moduli space $M_C(1-d, L)$ of rank 1 line bundles on $C$ with degree $d = 1 - g$. We establish that for every such semi-stable bundle $L$, the set of points on $C$ accessible via $L$—specifically, the set of points reachable through $L$—is infinite provided the degree $d$ satisfies $d \geq 1$.

Gravitational waves (GWs) are a cornerstone of multi-messenger astronomy, offering a unique window into the universe. While current research primarily focuses on detecting the leading post-Newtonian (PN) order modes, recent studies have identified higher-order modes (HOMs) as promising for future observations. This study investigates the observability of advanced-order modes (AOMs)—specifically the octupole ($l=3$) and $l=4$ modes—within the upcoming era of third-generation GW detectors. We demonstrate that these AOMs can be detected by both Cosmic Explorer (CE) and the Einstein Telescope (ET). Furthermore, we analyze the detectability of these modes across various source types, including binary black holes, neutron star mergers, and core-collapse supernovae. Our findings indicate that CE and ET will detect AOMs from binary black hole mergers with signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) ranging from 10 to 100, while detections from neutron star mergers and core-collapse supernovae will exhibit lower SNRs, falling between 5 and 20. Additionally, we calculated the detectability of the $l=3$ and $l=4$ modes for core-collapse supernovae at a distance of 10 kpc. The Gaia mission has identified numerous astrometric anomalies, some of which are attributed to the gravitational influence of unseen companions. This study examines the feasibility of characterizing such objects by utilizing partial astrometric data. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, significant insights into these hidden companions can be derived by analyzing the orbital trajectories of their visible counterparts. We introduce a novel method for estimating the mass of an invisible companion by leveraging the partial orbital path of its visible partner. This approach relies on the assumption that the visible body remains bound to its companion and that the companion's mass is negligible compared to the total system mass. We evaluate the accuracy of this method through simulations of hypothetical two-body systems, comparing our results against estimates generated by the Gaia Data Release 3 (GDR3) astrometric solution. Our findings indicate that the technique yields reliable mass estimates for unseen companions with masses exceeding 0.01 times the mass of the visible object, provided the visible object's mass is at least 0.1 times that of the Sun.

The 0/1 Knapsack problem is a well-known combinatorial optimization challenge that has been widely addressed using Genetic Algorithms (GA). This study evaluates the performance of various GA convergence strategies, specifically focusing on different combinations of selection and crossover methods. Experiments were conducted using three selection approaches—Roulette Wheel, Tournament, and Rank—paired with two crossover strategies, namely Uniform and Single Crossover. Results indicate that the Roulette Wheel selection method consistently outperforms both Tournament and Rank selection across all tested scenarios. Furthermore, the Uniform crossover operator was found to be more effective than single-crossover when working with selection methods based on tournament or rank.

This study examines $L^2$-norm estimates for a trilinear oscillatory integral in the convolution form, characterized by distinct smooth phase functions and two smooth amplitude functions. The analysis establishes that when there is no vanishing of oscillation at the origin, specific non-stationary conditions on the phase function ensure the integral is bounded in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$. Furthermore, for the case involving oscillation decay at the origin, we demonstrate that these $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ estimates hold universally regardless of the phase functions' specific forms.

Hatred is a prevalent and harmful phenomenon that demands immediate attention. This study introduces a new approach to detecting hate speech by employing the T5 framework, which is typically used for natural language processing tasks. We introduce an enhanced version of the Twitter dataset, specifically designed to address the limitations of existing public datasets. Our method involves a rigorous cleaning process to remove data points that do not align with hate speech classification, such as offensive but non-hate content, and spam. Furthermore, we utilize ensemble learning by integrating our T5-based model with other machine learning algorithms. Our findings demonstrate that this ensemble method outperforms the standalone T5 model.

This study examines the scaling attributes of the quantum Monte Carlo interaction model for heavy ions, specifically focusing on the computational efficiency of the algorithm. The results indicate that the model's efficiency is highly sensitive to the number of nucleons, with a computational cost that grows exponentially as this number increases. This exponential trend is attributed to the scaling of the system's basis set size.

The 2020 United States presidential election triggered a significant rise in Twitter activity regarding claims of fraud. This study examines the nature of this discourse by analyzing a collection of 11.5 million tweets from November 2020, which includes 1,000 assertions of election fraud and 1,000 counter-assertions. We categorize these claims based on their specific targets and content, revealing that while the vast majority of election-related Twitter activity consists of general rhetoric, specific fraud claims focus on three primary areas: voting procedures, vote counting, and electoral integrity. Furthermore, our analysis of the actors behind these narratives indicates that while regular users dominate the conversation, the most active fraud promoters are often verified political figures, whereas the most vigorous critics are typically journalists.

This work investigates the emergence of diffeomorphisms defined on a torus, a scenario where a linear drift vector field interferes with a small, nonlinear perturbation. We demonstrate that for each of these perturbed maps, there exists a solution forming a canonical torus; this object is a Lipschitz invariant torus characterized by maximal regularity, whose associated measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. This finding represents a significant advancement over the findings of Arnold and Rüssmann, as it applies to cases with non-vanishing positive Lyapunov exponents rather than requiring zero coefficients. Our methodology relies on the application of the KAM theorem to the corresponding normal form.

Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) are gaining significant traction in machine learning for their capacity to quantify uncertainty. Although they are theoretically robust, their practical application is hindered by the prohibitive computational costs associated with sampling-based inference methods. To address this, we introduce a novel BNN architecture designed to encode the posterior distribution directly, enabling uncertainty measurement without sampling. Our approach employs a two-stage training protocol: first, a standard BNN is trained via maximum likelihood estimation; second, a subsequent optimization phase adjusts the network's parameters to encode the posterior. We validate this method across various classification benchmarks and regression tasks, demonstrating that it achieves performance parity with traditional BNNs while maintaining efficiency.

This study presents a semiclassical instanton treatment of Marcus-Levich-Jortner (MLJ) theory, which addresses electron transfer within environments characterized by both harmonic oscillators and phonons. By applying the WKB approximation to the path integral formulation, we derive a semiclassical expression for the MLJ rate constant. This formulation incorporates a one-dimensional instanton action governing electron transfer and a multidimensional instanton action representing the environmental response. We demonstrate that the semiclassical approach yields identical results to the original MLJ theory, with the latter emerging as a specific case where quantum tunneling effects are neglected. Furthermore, we extend this semiclassical formalism to include pure quantum effects, establishing a systematic methodology for calculating MLJ rate constants that bridges classical and quantum regimes.

This study introduces a mixed control design framework for robotic manipulators, integrating the strengths of both passivity-based and adaptive control strategies. The proposed method ensures asymptotic convergence along a desired trajectory, even in the presence of unmodeled nonlinearities, unbalanced uncertainties, and external disturbances. Furthermore, the mixed design allows for the derivation of exponential rates of convergence for exponential tracking errors, provided that certain conditions on the unmodeled nonlinearities are met. The efficacy of this hybrid controller is substantiated through simulations involving a two-link robotic manipulator.

We introduce a theory describing the vast thermoelectric effect (VTE), a phenomenon where a temperature gradient applied to a small area of a magnetic material generates a substantial electric field. This effect arises from the rapid transfer of heat energy into magnons near the hot spot, followed by their slow diffusion across the bulk material. The resulting VTE efficiency is quantified by a coefficient $\alpha_E$, which is derived from the magnon thermal conductivity $\kappa_m$, electron-magnon coupling strength $g$, and spin Hall angle $\theta_{SH}$. The formula is expressed as $\alpha_E = g^2 \theta_{SH} \kappa_m / (2 \sigma T)$, where $\sigma$ denotes electrical conductivity and $T$ represents temperature. The study also examines the effect's dependence on magnetic properties and temperature, alongside an analysis of the potential for achieving large $\alpha_E$ values in Heusler alloys.
This paper presents a stochastic approach to resolve the problem of determining the ideal sum.

This study examines the component structure of finite field binomials of the form $f(x) = x^d-ax^m-a$, where $a$ is a nonzero element of the field $K$. The primary objective is to determine the number of unipotent elements in the component group of the ideal generated by $f(x)$, which is equivalent to the number of monic irreducible factors of $f(x)$ in $K$. We establish that the component group consists of exactly one unipotent element if and only if $d$ is a prime number. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the component group contains precisely two unipotent elements if and only if $d$ is a composite number and $a$ is a primitive element. Finally, we derive a lower bound for the count of unipotent components.

UPAAL is a widely recognized tool for modeling and analyzing non-deterministic, timed, and concurrent systems. It enables the specification of system behaviors using network diagrams, which are then validated against various temporal logic properties. Beyond verification, the tool offers a suite of services, including simulation, model checking, and the generation of counterexamples. This paper presents a practical case study in which the PUPAAL tool was employed to verify a real-world implementation of a digital circuit.

We introduce a novel, end-to-end deep learning framework that jointly optimizes the design of metasurface masks and the image reconstruction process. By treating the mask as a learnable parameter, our approach integrates the physical optics of light propagation directly with the image recovery stage. This unified architecture significantly accelerates the training process and ensures the solution aligns with the specific physical constraints of the optical system. The resulting method demonstrates superior image recovery accuracy compared to reconstruction techniques that separate mask design and image recovery into distinct steps.

This study examines the temporal evolution of the AC-Stark effect within a framework of intense bi-color circularly polarized laser fields. We demonstrate that a specific frequency offset between the two circular components induces a periodic AC-Stark shift, a phenomenon we term "AC-Stark displacement." This occurrence arises from the modulation of the field's ellipticity. Our findings are corroborated through numerical simulations, which reveal that electron recollision energies are significantly modulated by this displacement effect.

This paper introduces a new automatic photo-blending system that constructs a composite image by merging semantic components from two distinct source photos. To achieve this, the system first segments both source images into their respective semantic parts, then recombines these elements to form a novel scene, and finally synthesizes a unified output. This research advances the field of automatic photo blending by tackling the inherent complexities of both semantic segmentation and photo blending. We specifically develop semantic photo blending methods that utilize a newly designed neural network architecture, incorporating specialized modules for both semantic segmentation and photo blending. The results indicate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in generating high-quality blended images.

The dynamics of gene expression are governed by intricate biochemical processes that generate stochastic time series. This study introduces a methodology for extracting data from such series, utilizing a hidden Markov model (HMM) to segment time series into distinct states. This approach is applied to a two-gene network, where the identified states correspond to distinct expression patterns. We demonstrate that this technique can effectively recover the underlying parameters of a gene network model, even when the HMM-derived states do not perfectly align with the true dynamic trajectories generated by the system.

This study introduces an innovative, data-driven semi-supervised approach to education, leveraging the inherent dynamics of the learning process. By employing a two-tiered neural network architecture, the model functions simultaneously as a curriculum planner and an instruction generator. The upper layer constructs a curriculum by identifying the most suitable data points for the lower network, which in turn produces instructional data tailored to that specific curriculum. A key advantage of this framework is its ability to adapt to individual student needs, thereby enhancing learning efficiency. Additionally, the model's capacity to generate instructional data enables the creation of interactive educational content, such as animated simulations for science learning.

Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms (QAOA) are variational methods designed to address combinatorial optimization tasks, but their performance is often hindered by training overload, a phenomenon where the training landscape becomes increasingly complex as the problem size grows. This study investigates the impact of training overload on QAOA using the Max-Cut problem as a case study. We demonstrate that QAOA's efficacy is constrained by the depth of its circuit architecture; specifically, beyond a critical threshold, further increasing the circuit depth yields diminishing returns. Furthermore, we establish that this performance plateau occurs at progressively shallower circuit depths when problem sizes increase. These findings underscore the significance of training overload in limiting QAOA's practical utility and suggest that optimizing the circuit depth for specific problem scales is essential for maximizing performance.

Re-identification involves retrieving a specific target individual from multiple camera networks based on visual cues, a task that has garnered significant attention. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel framework for the inverse problem: identifying a specific person across different camera networks from a set of known reference images. We present a new method that leverages the shared semantic attributes of the person, utilizing a dual-stage architecture. First, a self-attention-based multi-branch deep learning model extracts distinctive features from the person and surrounding context. Second, a dedicated re-identification module refines these features to pinpoint the target. We validate our approach on the challenging Person-2-All dataset, demonstrating that it surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

The integration of renewable energy sources into the power grid has led to increased variability and uncertainty, necessitating robust research and development of advanced control and planning strategies. However, the limited availability of extensive, high-quality datasets hinders progress in this area. This paper introduces a data-informed approach to time series reconstruction for power systems, utilizing limited historical data to generate synthetic sequences that honor the statistical characteristics of the original series. By analyzing the empirical distribution function (EDF) of historical load and generation data, we identify key statistical properties and employ a generative adversarial network (GAN) to synthesize new data that maintains these features. Furthermore, we propose a new GAN architecture capable of generating multi-variable time series, such as those found in multi-area systems, ensuring inter-area statistical dependencies are preserved. This method offers a flexible and effective solution for generating power system time series, with potential applications in control, planning, and broader system research.

This paper introduces a robust-convergence-friendly modified algorithm designed to identify a unique solution to a variational inequality problem. The proposed operator-based method incorporates modifications to iterates, ensuring robust convergence even when dealing with general monotone operators. Furthermore, we examine the scenario where these operators exhibit either strict or uniform strong monotonicity.

This study investigates the intersection count of closed geodesics within certain compact Riemann surface-embedded Fuchsian frameworks. We establish an upper limit on these crossings for specific surface types, leveraging this to prove the existence of isoxial groups for those cases. Conversely, by applying the Schottky method we demonstrate the presence of isoxial groups in specific scenarios, which allows us to derive lower bounds on geodesic crossings for said instances.

This study examines the potential Lepton Flavor Violation (LFV) decay mode $\Upsilon (3S)\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\pm}$ within the framework of the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (THDM). We calculate the branching fraction for this process, comparing THDM results with those from the Standard Model (SM) to determine the sensitivity of $\Upsilon (3S)$ decays to LFV. Our analysis indicates that the branching fraction for $\Upsilon (3S)\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\pm}$ in the THDM is significantly higher than in the SM, with the THDM value being approximately $10^4$ times greater. We further evaluate the feasibility of detecting this decay at the Fermilab Tevatron and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

The search for new superconductors with critical temperatures ($T_c$) exceeding room temperature remains a significant challenge in condensed matter physics. In this study, we demonstrate that applying high pressure can significantly enhance superconductivity in a flat-band Kagome system, Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$. Our findings reveal that the superconducting $T_c$ increases from 1.2 K at ambient conditions to 2.5 K at 10 GPa, a rise that correlates with the suppression of the structural transition from a low-temperature monoclinic phase to a high-temperature orthorhombic phase. Additionally, we observe a strong pressure-induced enhancement in the electronic density of states (DOS) at the Fermi level, which we attribute to the reduction in lattice volume. These results indicate that the mechanism driving superconductivity in Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ is closely linked to the volume expansion of the lattice and the associated increase in DOS.

We examine how data regarding a black hole can be recovered in Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity. The analysis begins by establishing the connection between the boundary conformal field theory and the near-horizon region of the black hole. Subsequently, we derive the two-point correlation function for the near-horizon geometry, demonstrating that it aligns with the form predicted by the conformal field theory located on the boundary.

This study investigates the application of Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (NODE) models to scenarios where data is characterized by erratic and noisy conditions. Specifically, we examine two setups: one involving the retrieval of a hidden state from noisy observations, and the other predicting future states from current observations. The first scenario is analyzed using a Kalman filter, while the second employs a Kalman integrator. The research further explores the dynamics of the hidden state under noisy conditions, focusing on two distinct noise types: (i) noise that fluctuates randomly, and (ii) noise that varies systematically. We also analyze the impact of noise on the hidden state itself, considering both random and systematic variations. The findings demonstrate that NODE models can effectively handle these noisy environments, provided the hidden state is not subjected to systematic noise.

This study introduces the Object Recall Transformer (ORTR), a transformer-based architecture designed for object-driven navigation. ORTR operates by processing a sequence of visual observations and object concepts to generate a sequence of control commands. Central to this approach is the ORTR's ability to recall objects from past observations, thereby enabling the agent to effectively pursue its goals. Additionally, the model employs a novel "dynamic window" mechanism to ensure long-term planning and efficient navigation. Empirical evaluations across three distinct object-target navigation tasks demonstrate that ORTR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior performance in terms of both sample efficiency and final task success rates.

Recent research indicates that large language models (LLMs) can acquire the ability to follow instructions through meta-learning, a process termed Instruction Meta-Learning (IML). However, the computational demands of IML are substantial, necessitating the utilization of massive datasets and powerful hardware. This paper introduces OPT-IML, a novel framework designed to scale IML effectively. By leveraging the generalization capabilities of pre-trained LMs, OPT-IML employs a two-stage strategy: first, it utilizes a pre-trained model to forecast the optimal output distribution for a specific instruction; second, it applies gradient descent to fine-tune the model's parameters directly on the loss computed from this predicted distribution. This approach significantly reduces the computational costs associated with training. We evaluate OPT-IML against IML on the Instruction Tuning Benchmark (ITB) using both the OPT-110B and OPT-30B models. Our results demonstrate that OPT-IML achieves performance comparable to IML while reducing the total training cost by 90%.

Scratch serves as a widely adopted, visual programming environment designed to foster computational thinking, digital literacy, and creative coding. It stands as one of the most prevalent platforms on the Scratch Education Portal, hosting millions of user projects. While the platform's official mission is to enable users to create and share interactive stories, games, and art, it also supports a wide array of unofficial applications, including data visualization, social network analysis, and the development of educational tools. This paper presents a quantitative investigation into how Scratch's inherent features facilitate these diverse uses. By analyzing the platform's architectural design, we demonstrate that its flexibility allows users to achieve numerous goals through various pathways. This adaptability is a critical factor in Scratch's enduring success and widespread adoption.

This study calculates the linear response of a uniform electron fluid to perturbations, employing the Jastrow-projected correlated wavefunction of the Ceperley and Alder variational Monte Carlo method. The results demonstrate that incorporating correlation effects into linear response theory significantly enhances the accuracy of computed dielectric functions. Furthermore, we establish that the calculated energy-loss function aligns closely with the experimental electron energy-loss spectrum observed in solid argon.

We introduce a method for generating physically constrained synthetic data by utilizing position uncertainty information. Our approach employs optimal transport to map the probability density of positional uncertainty onto the original dataset, creating a transport map that applies to each sample to produce a corresponding synthetic counterpart. This technique allows for the rapid generation of large-scale datasets, and we have validated its effectiveness on a real-world particle physics application.

The rapid proliferation of Big Data has spurred the creation of numerous platforms designed to facilitate data sharing and analysis. Nevertheless, the sensitive nature of this information has intensified the need for robust safeguards to protect it. Consequently, there is a pressing demand for advanced privacy-preserving techniques that can effectively secure Big Data. This paper introduces a novel distributed tensor computation method designed to enable collaborative Big Data analysis while ensuring data privacy. The proposed approach leverages tensor network decomposition techniques to enforce privacy protection. Specifically, the method employs randomized tensor network decomposition to anonymize tensor data, thereby preserving its essential statistical properties. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the accuracy of Big Data analysis remains intact even after such anonymization. Finally, the study outlines a distributed computation framework for Big Data analysis that integrates the proposed randomized decomposition method.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven highly effective for training robots to execute complex tasks. However, the significant gap between simulated and real-world environments often hinders the direct transfer of this knowledge. To bridge this gap, researchers have developed sim2real transfer techniques, yet these methods frequently compromise safety and security. This paper introduces SafeAPT, a secure and robust framework designed to ensure safe and effective policy transfer from simulation to reality. SafeAPT operates by generating a diverse set of policies within the simulation, each optimized for distinct reward functions. These varied policies are then deployed on the physical robot, where the system continuously monitors their performance and safety. By leveraging this pool of options, SafeAPT can dynamically select the most appropriate policy to handle real-world uncertainties, thereby enhancing both safety and adaptability. The proposed method is validated through a real robot door-opening task, demonstrating its ability to successfully transfer and adapt policies across different environments.

This study examines the observational characteristics of jets within radio galaxies and quasars, with a specific focus on the mechanisms driving their collimation and the physical processes responsible for their energy dissipation. We explore the hypothesis that jets are confined by the surrounding interstellar medium, which is a model consistent with observations of jets in both young and mature galaxies. Furthermore, we analyze the dissipation of jet kinetic energy, proposing that this occurs through interactions with the ambient interstellar medium. We discuss the resulting radio lobes and their morphology, as well as the generation of large-scale shocks within these jets and at their terminus, which are responsible for the observed synchrotron radiation.

This study addresses time-varying non-linear regression with multiple responses, where the underlying functional form shifts over time. We introduce a method that concurrently employs sieve estimation to learn evolving regression curves while adaptively identifying an evolving set of active basis functions. The approach constructs a time-dependent, sparse basis for each outcome, enabling the estimation of a time-varying sparse partial differential equation (PDE) that governs the time-varying evolution of the function. We establish theoretical convergence rates for both the estimated functions and the identified time-varyening active sets, accounting for the inherent sparsity of the latter. Simulation results demonstrate that the method effectively recovers time-varyening sparse non-linear relationships and outperforms existing approaches in both accuracy and set recovery.

This paper examines the effectiveness of various neural architectures for identifying aggressive speech within the SemEval-2017 Task 4 framework. We introduce a new, highly efficient approach that leverages Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to process raw audio waveforms, achieving a 2.5% relative improvement in F1-score over the top performing traditional feature-based system. Additionally, we conduct an analysis of various neural models trained on different feature sets, revealing that CNNs utilizing raw waveforms consistently outperform other architectures across all categories.

Functional connectivity (FC) within the human brain is a critical area of neuroscience research, with recent interest in applying deep learning to analyze resting-state fMRI data. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to extract discriminative features from FC patterns, enabling the identification of distinct clinical conditions. The approach utilizes a hybrid architecture combining a graph convolutional network (GCN) and a deep neural network (DNN). Specifically, the GCN isolates discriminative connectivity features, which are subsequently processed by the DNN to generate classification outcomes. Validated against a dataset comprising 1,000 subjects with varying diagnoses, the method achieved an average accuracy of 84.4% in condition identification. Additionally, the identified connectivity features were mapped to brain regions, revealing patterns that align with existing scientific knowledge.

This study introduces a new approach to analyzing the convergence of algorithms for solving monotone inclusions, building upon Nesterov's enhanced technique. By utilizing a framework of maximal monotone operators, we demonstrate that this enhanced method maintains dissipativity. This property enables the construction of a Lyapunov function, which proves global convergence for the algorithm. Furthermore, our analysis confirms that Nesterov's enhanced technique achieves convergence rates superior to those of the standard forward-backward splitting method.

This study introduces a new numerical framework for solving hyperbolic systems with source terms using an implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta method. The approach relies on an operator-splitting technique applied to the time integration, where the source term component is handled implicitly and the wave propagation part explicitly. To address boundaries within a finite volume context, we integrate a fictitious domain method with a fictitious boundary closure scheme. This setup imposes specific conditions at the artificial limits to ensure proper interaction between the wave equations and source terms. The method's accuracy and stability are validated through various test cases, including the Riemann problem, the 1D Sod shock tube, and the 1D Burgers equation.
